grammar.title: 9A: Third conditional
grammar.explanation:
We use the third conditional to talk about the past. We imagine how the past could have been different.

We build it with **if + past perfect** in one half, and **would have + past participle** in the other half.

Example: *If I had charged my phone, I would have taken more photos.* I did not charge it, so I took no photos.

We never say ~~if I would have~~. The word **would** goes in the second half only.

We can use **might have** or **could have** instead of **would have** when the result is less sure. *If she had clicked send, he might have seen the file.*

The short form 'd means two things. In the if-half it means **had**: *If I'd known*. In the other half it means **would**: *I'd have helped you*.
examples: *If I had uploaded the file, you would have seen my photos.* (I did not upload it, so you saw nothing.)
*If she had clicked the right button, the app would have opened.* (She clicked the wrong button.)
*If he had looked at the screen, he would have read my message.* (He never looked at the screen.)
*If we had bought a smart TV, we would have watched the match together.* (We stayed home.)
*If I'd saved my data, I wouldn't have lost my work.* (I lost all my data.)
*If they had brought a camera, they could have filmed the wedding.* (They brought no camera.)

practice.q: Make a third conditional: I did not charge my phone. I missed the call.
practice.a: If I had charged my phone, I would not have missed the call.

practice.q: Is this correct: 'If I would have known, I would have come'? Fix it if not.
practice.a: Not correct. Say: 'If I had known, I would have come.'

practice.q: What does this mean: 'If I'd studied harder, I might have passed'?
practice.a: I did not study hard, and maybe I failed. The result is less certain, so we use 'might have'.
